top.title: Distant time crystals oscillate in unison, paving the way for spin networks
top.summary: In January 2024, physicists at TU Dortmund University demonstrated a continuous time crystal in a semiconductor whose oscillations remained stable for hours. more.title: When meat doesn't matter: Female Guinea baboons do not prefer males who are better at acquiring or sharing meat
more.summary: Meat is a rare and highly prized resource for wild Guinea baboons (Papio papio). Yet, contrary to long-standing assumptions based on human hunter–gatherer societies, a new study by the German Primate Center—Leibniz-Institute for Primate Research (DPZ) reveals that female Guinea baboons do not preferentially choose males who are more skilled at acquiring meat as their mates.

more.title: Mars could have carried liquid water more recently than we thought
more.summary: For decades, astronomers have assumed that the Martian surface froze solid around 3 billion years ago and has stayed that way ever since. If this were really the case, any liquid water would have long since either been locked away underground or lost to space.

more.title: Why Are Rivers So Mathematical?
more.author: Natalie Wolchover
more.summary: A simple scaling law brings order to the chaos of flowing water, rock, and sediment. New findings have extended the law even further. The post Why Are Rivers So Mathematical? first appeared on Quanta Magazine

more.title: Global New Unicorn Counts In The First Half Of 2026 Have Already Surpassed 2025’s Totals
more.author: Gené Teare
more.summary: A total 195 companies joined The Crunchbase Unicorn Board in the first half of 2026 — far surpassing counts seen since the second half of 2022. Already, H1 is above the new unicorn totals for all of 2025, when 193 companies were minted with that status.

more.title: Ancient Maltese seafarers likely navigated by the stars
more.summary: Malta might be the last place one would expect a convergence of archeoastronomy and early cosmology. Today, it's better known as a billionaire tax haven and a favorite production location for big-budget Hollywood movies.

more.title: Microplastics may transport hazardous plastic additives through marine environments
more.summary: Plastic pollution is not only a marine litter issue; it is also closely linked to resource circulation and chemical management. Plastic products contain a wide range of additives, including antioxidants, plasticizers, ultraviolet stabilizers and flame retardants. Some of these chemicals are regulated or managed because of concerns about their effects on human health and ecosystems.

more.title: Scientific advancement has never been more prolific—so why has trust in science plummeted?
more.summary: From genome editing to quantum computing, scientific progress is accelerating at an unprecedented pace, yet public faith in science is collapsing. Our species has mapped the human genome, created powerful computers that sit in the palms of our hands and extended human life spans beyond what our ancestors could have imagined—meanwhile, anti-intellectual movements are gaining momentum.

more.title: Scientists discover a hidden switch inside silver nanocatalysts
more.summary: Silver nanocatalysts have been found to switch where they perform their most important reactions depending on whether a solid oxide cell is making electricity or hydrogen. The discovery could enable smarter catalyst designs that boost clean power generation while making green hydrogen more energy-efficient.

more.title: Discovered Materials is playing AI whack-a-mole to hunt cooler chips
more.author: Tim Fernholz
more.summary: Discovered Materials raised $9 million to fund the hunt for more novel materials to build more efficient chips.

more.title: Report confirms record-high greenhouse gases, global sea level and ocean heat in 2025
more.summary: According to the 36th annual State of the Climate report, greenhouse gas concentrations, global sea level and ocean heat content all reached record highs in 2025.

more.title: Traditional plastic forks shed harmful microplastics. Plastic created from sugar is an alternative
more.summary: At a Massachusetts lab, pebble-sized pellets are transformed into forks and films that won't leave persistent microplastics in the environment.

more.title: 240-million-year-old reptile fossil reveals a lost chapter before dinosaurs and crocodiles
more.summary: A 240-million-year-old reptile discovered in Brazil is revealing what evolution looked like just before the rise of dinosaurs and crocodiles. The small predator had unusually positioned legs that may have allowed it to move more efficiently than many earlier reptiles.

more.title: Oak leaves harbor distinct microbial worlds on their opposite surfaces
more.summary: A single leaf may look like a simple patch of green, but to the microscopic life that inhabits it, it is a vast landscape divided into different worlds.

more.title: Peer review is overwhelmed—can it survive in the AI era?
more.author: Saima Sidik
more.summary: As research and AI-assisted papers surge, volunteer reviewers struggle to keep up.

more.title: US had hottest month on record in July
more.summary: July 2026 marked the hottest month on record for the contiguous United States, the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration said Monday, continuing a recent trend driven by human-caused climate change.

more.title: DNA repair enzymes favor specific sequences, shaping mutation patterns in the human genome
more.summary: When a wound does not heal properly, it leaves a scar. Similarly, mutations—which are permanent changes to genetic code—are often the result of damaged DNA that has not been properly repaired. Mutations can impede the function of genes and lead to disease and aging, but they are also the source of genetic variation, which allows new traits to emerge and facilitates the evolutionary process.

more.title: Drought dries major European rivers to record lows
more.summary: Vast tracts of many of Europe's largest rivers, including the Rhine, Rhone and Danube, have slowed to a trickle never before recorded in July, data from a European climate observatory showed Monday.

more.title: Engineered enzymes forge carbon-carbon and carbon-nitrogen bonds with high selectivity
more.summary: Researchers from the Manchester Institute of Biotechnology, including Dr. Zachary Birch-Price and professor Anthony Green, have developed a new family of engineered enzymes that can create several different types of chemical bonds used to build complex molecules.

more.title: When it comes to predicting people's preferences, it pays to consider 'the power of three'
more.summary: In his 1927 paper, "A law of comparative judgment," the American psychologist L. L. Thurstone proposed that when people select one option among multiple alternatives, they are picking the one that has the highest value to them, even though they cannot assign a particular number to that choice.

more.title: The sediment story: A journey that impacts India's rivers and surrounding landscapes
more.summary: Every monsoon, India's rivers turn brown. To most of us, that color simply means muddy water. But hidden within it is the material that builds fertile floodplains, creates river islands, nourishes deltas and even shapes coastlines: sediment.

more.title: Water quality, not just scarcity, may shape future competition for a limited resource
more.summary: Climate change is largely to blame for water scarcity. The low water levels in European rivers this summer speak volumes in that respect.
